title: Chronicle admission thermostat and attention reservoir for tail-latency smoothing
creator: Maya Singh
description: Replace the current coarse-grained admission + batch-shaping heuristic with a two-tier runtime controller: a short-horizon "thermostat" that reacts to instantaneous latency pressure and a longer-horizon "attention reservoir" that reserves prefills/kernels for predicted high-cost requests. The goal is to reduce 99th/99.9th token latency by smoothing admission at both prefill and decode stages and improving kernel selection for heterogeneous workloads.
goal: Reduce tail token latency (p99/p99.9) by at least 25% in mixed short/long request workloads without increasing median latency by more than 5% and maintain or improve GPU utilization.
scope: Runtime admission logic, batch shaper, kernel hinting interface, attention prefetch reservoir. Does NOT include new kernel implementations or model architecture changes. Integrations: console SLO dashboards and A/B rollout hooks.
proposed_solution: Introduce two coordinated runtime components: (1) Chronicle Thermostat — a rapid-feedback controller that adjusts instant admission rates and transient batch caps using EWMA of token latencies and queue depths; (2) Attention Reservoir — a predictive quota system that tags incoming prefill requests with 'attention credit' budget based on token-length forecasts, recent cache hits, and kernel cost estimates. The runtime uses kernel cost model table (compiled offline) to choose kernel variant and to charge reservoir credits. Admission decisions consult both components: thermostat enforces short-term caps, reservoir enforces budgeted long-run fairness across tenants/priority classes.
design_decisions: Use EWMA(α=0.25) window for thermostat latency signal to react within ~3 samples
Encode per-kernel cost estimates as tokens-per-ms and store in a versioned catalog referenced by runtime
Reservoir credits are integer-valued; larger-decoder requests debit more credits enabling predictable budget tracking
Admission controllers run in the serving runtime process with lock-free read paths and a single writer token to update policy snapshots
Fallback path: if reservoir snapshot unavailable, use conservative thermostat-only mode to avoid over-commit
success_metrics: p99 token latency reduction >= 25% on mixed-short-long benchmark (latency-lab/mix-1)
median token latency change between -5% and +5%
GPU utilization >= baseline or improved cost per token
No increase in error rate or incorrect kernel selection incidents
rollout_plan: 1) Implement controllers behind runtime feature flag
2) Canary on 5% traffic for non-critical tenants with telemetry collection
3) Evaluate metrics for 48h: latency curves, admission rate logs, kernel-selection distribution
4) Expand to 25% with additional watchdog thresholds (if p99 spikes >10% revert)
5) Full rollout with soft A/B comparing cost/token and latency over one week
6) Post-rollout: promote new kernel cost catalog to production and enable console reporting
risks: Over-aggressive reservoir policy could starve bursty low-priority workloads; mitigate with min-allowance floor
Incorrect kernel cost estimates could bias admission leading to worse latency — require offline calibration and continuous re-measure
Concurrency bugs in runtime controller causing inconsistent admissions across shards — add thorough fuzz tests and replica consistency checks
Telemetry volume increase from admission tracing — add sampling and aggregation to avoid metrics pressure
comments: 2025-11-05 Maya Singh: Initial spike test with conservative thermostat delta=0.1 looked promising — p99 down ~15% on stubbed kernels.
2025-11-07 Ari Kaplan: Implemented reservoir proto and local simulation harness. Observed starvation for size-1 low-priority requests; added min-allowance and duty-cycle refill.
2025-11-09 Rajiv Patel: Reviewed kernel cost catalog format; suggested adding per-sequence-length interpolation to avoid stair-step artifacts.
2025-11-10 Ops Alert: Canary run at 5% showed reduced p99 but a spike on region-eu-west-1 during GC events. We've added GC-aware backoff to thermostat.
